chunks.text:
Content-addressed storage gives an object a key derived from its bytes. In a simple store, the key is $k=H(b)$, where $b$ is the stored byte string and $H$ is a cryptographic hash function.1 To check a retrieved object, hash its bytes and compare the result with the requested key. This checks that the object matches the key; deciding which key to trust is a separate problem.
An ISBN identifies a publication’s title, edition and format. It is assigned through a publishing system, so it cannot verify a downloaded book’s bytes.

What it identifies




Content key
An object encoded with a particular hashing scheme. Its bytes can be checked against the key.


Location, such as a URL used over HTTP
A place to request a resource. The response can change while the URL stays the same.



A hash has a fixed number of possible outputs, so collisions exist. A suitable cryptographic hash makes finding a collision impractical under its security assumptions. It also lets identical encoded objects share a key, which supports deduplication. The key alone provides no storage capacity or availability: some store or peer still has to retain and serve the object.
In IPFS, a CID includes format and hash information. A file may be split into blocks and represented by a DAG, so its root CID generally differs from a hash of the raw file bytes. Chunking and encoding settings affect that root.
Immutable Objects, Mutable References
In a Merkle DAG, nodes contain links to their children by content key. Editing a child changes its key, assuming no collision. Updating the parent’s link then changes the parent’s key, continuing up to the root. Unchanged nodes can be shared between versions. The Merkle DAG structure makes each root identify a particular version.
A mutable reference supplies the name for the latest version. Publish a new root, then update that reference. IPNS uses signed records for this purpose. Readers must verify the reference’s authority and freshness; old content keys still refer to the old objects for as long as those objects remain available.
See also IPFS, Block-reference mechanism
